Topic:AFL Women’s

Caitlin Reid is one of dozens of female athletes juggling two jobs in the AFLW. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

When Caitlin Reid is not re-arranging her patient's vital organs you will find her on the training field.

Such is life for many professional female athletes, whose sporting income falls short of providing a sustainable living.

"A lot of us [AFLW players] don't earn enough to survive on the footy alone," she said.

The 29-year-old's typical day starts from first light at the SCG working on her ruck craft with the football.

After midday is usually when she heads off to St Vincent's Hospital to start her shift as a surgical registrar working on the frontline of patient care.

"I'm usually working if not seven days a week, six days a week," Reid said.

Caitlin Reid trains with the Sydney Swans several days a week while balancing her job as a surgical registrar. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Growing up, girls' football didn't exist for Reid. It was not until halfway through her medical degree that she discovered the league.

Initially the tall ruck said her passion was in basketball, but COVID cancelled the NBL1 star's season with the Albury Wodonga bandits.

So Reid took a chance playing in an AFL Nines competition to maintain her fitness through the season.

"By the time basketball was ready to go back I loved footy more than I loved basketball," she said.

Emily Pease followed her two passions in football and love for animals to get the best of both worlds. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Emily Pease is performing the same juggling act as a winger for GWS while wrangling wildlife at Sydney's Taronga zoo.

"It's my double life. I'll start with meetings, a gym session and a field session with the Giants, then flip it to the zoo greeting guests and interacting with the animals," Pease said.

"It's actually really cool having footy life and also having something outside of it which I'm really passionate about."

The 24-year-old started playing Aussie rules in Canberra and had the opportunity to train with the Giants academy before making her way to the team.

GWS Giants winger Emily Pease trains several days a week while balancing her job at Taronga Zoo. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Most of her co-workers at the zoo do not know about her double life.

"A lot of my colleagues kind of just go 'wow'. No-one really expects that I'm playing footy. It's like I'm revealing a superpower," Pease said.

She hopes to be a full-time zookeeper one day, preferably working with primates.

According to data, the average wage of an AFLW player in the 2026 season is $79,414. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

The latest data from the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) tracked that 3 per cent of AFLW players work full-time outside of playing on the field, down from 6 per cent last year.

Across 540 listed players in the women's league an additional 62 per cent work part-time or casual jobs.

And according to AFLPA data, the average wage of an AFLW player in the 2026 season is $79,414.

From 2027 AFLW players will move from the current four-tier system pay to a salary cap model similar to the men. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"Some people ask why I do both jobs. I think for me it's a bit of an outlet," Pease said.

"I'm able to take my mind off footy when I'm at the zoo and vice versa.

"I think just being given the opportunity to follow my passions. I had a passion for footy and for animals".

Reid has not had a holiday in two and half years, not because she does not want to, but because she has used most of her annual leave to accommodate her other career.

The five-year collective bargaining agreement covering male and female players features significant wage rises and a longer AFLW season.

"There's certainly an element of guilt I feel playing football because I'm not at the hospital and we are short-staffed as is everywhere in New South Wales," Reid said.

"My co-workers have to work extra hours because I'm not there. I love my job at the hospital but I also love my job at the club.

"I've said it before, medicine is a team sport and the closeness you feel towards your footy teammates is the closeness I feel towards my co-workers."

The 11th AFLW season begins this Sunday with a clash between St Kilda and Carlton at Docklands Stadium.
